section.title: The Allotment for Judah
section.sectionRationale: Judah, the royal tribe from which Messiah will come, receives its inheritance first and largest. The chapter maps Judah's borders, tells the vivid story of Caleb taking Hebron and Othniel winning Acsah and her springs, and lists Judah's many cities in every region, closing with an honest admission: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem. It is one movement, the allotment for Judah, in which God's faithfulness in giving the land meets Israel's incomplete obedience at the very city where the King will one day reign.
section.thesis: Judah, the tribe of the coming King, receives a full and detailed inheritance from the faithful hand of God, and within it faith is rewarded as Caleb and Othniel take their portions, yet the closing note that the Jebusites remained in Jerusalem quietly exposes the incompleteness of Israel's obedience, a gap only the true Son of Judah will finally close.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Judah's boundaries, verses 1 to 12; Caleb's conquest and Acsah's springs, verses 13 to 19; the cities of Judah region by region, verses 20 to 62; and the Jebusites left in Jerusalem, verse 63.

units.label: Judah's boundaries
units.note: the allotment for the tribe of Judah

verses.text: Now the allotment for the clans of the tribe of Judah extended to the border of Edom, to the Wilderness of Zin at the extreme southern boundary:
Their southern border started at the bay on the southern tip of the Salt Sea,
proceeded south of the Ascent of Akrabbim, continued on to Zin, went over to the south of Kadesh-barnea, ran past Hezron up to Addar, and curved toward Karka.
It proceeded to Azmon, joined the Brook of Egypt, and ended at the Sea. This was their southern border.
The eastern border was the Salt Sea as far as the mouth of the Jordan. The northern border started from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan,
went up to Beth-hoglah, proceeded north of Beth-arabah, and went up to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.

Then the border went up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, turning north to Gilgal, which faces the Ascent of Adummim south of the ravine. It continued along the waters of En-shemesh and came out at En-rogel.

From there the border went up the Valley of Ben-hinnom along the southern slope of the Jebusites (that is, Jerusalem) and ascended to the top of the hill that faces the Valley of Hinnom on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.
From the hilltop the border curved to the spring of the Waters of Nephtoah, proceeded to the cities of Mount Ephron, and then bent around toward Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).
The border curled westward from Baalah to Mount Seir, ran along the northern slope of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), went down to Beth-shemesh, and crossed to Timnah.
Then it went out to the northern slope of Ekron, curved toward Shikkeron, proceeded to Mount Baalah, went on to Jabneel, and ended at the Sea.
And the western border was the coastline of the Great Sea. These are the boundaries around the clans of the descendants of Judah.

units.label: Caleb's conquest and Acsah's springs
units.note: give me springs of water as well

verses.text: According to the LORD’s command to him, Joshua gave Caleb son of Jephunneh a portion among the sons of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron. (Arba was the forefather of Anak.)
And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
From there he marched against the inhabitants of Debir (formerly known as Kiriath-sepher).
And Caleb said, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.”
So Othniel son of Caleb’s brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage.
One day Acsah came to Othniel and urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got off her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you desire?”
“Give me a {{berakhah|blessing}},” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs.

units.label: The cities of Judah region by region
units.note: the inheritance of the tribe of Judah

verses.text: This is the {{nachalah|inheritance}} of the clans of the tribe of Judah.
These were the southernmost cities of the tribe of Judah in the Negev toward the border of Edom: Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,
Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,
Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,
Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,
Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),
Amam, Shema, Moladah,
Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet,
Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah,
Baalah, Iim, Ezem,
Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,
Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,
Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon, twenty-nine cities in all, along with their villages.
These were in the foothills: Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,
Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam,
Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,
Shaaraim, Adithaim, and Gederah (or Gederothaim), fourteen cities, along with their villages.
Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,
Dilan, Mizpeh, Joktheel,
Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,
Cabbon, Lahmas, Chitlish,
Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah, sixteen cities, along with their villages.
Libnah, Ether, Ashan,
Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,
Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah, nine cities, along with their villages.
Ekron, with its towns and villages;
from Ekron to the sea, all the cities near Ashdod, along with their villages;
Ashdod, with its towns and villages; Gaza, with its towns and villages, as far as the Brook of Egypt and the coastline of the Great Sea.
These were in the hill country: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,
Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),
Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,
Goshen, Holon, and Giloh, eleven cities, along with their villages.
Arab, Dumah, Eshan,
Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,
Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior, nine cities, along with their villages.
Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,
Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,
Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah, ten cities, along with their villages.
Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,
Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon, six cities, along with their villages.
Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah, two cities, along with their villages.
These were in the wilderness: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,
Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En-gedi, six cities, along with their villages.

units.label: The Jebusites left in Jerusalem
units.note: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites

verses.text: But the descendants of Judah could not {{yarash|drive out}} the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah.

berakhah.gloss: Blessing, a gift of favor and good. Acsah asks her father for a berakhah, and specifically for springs of water to make her dry Negev land fruitful. Her bold, believing request, and Caleb's generous granting of both upper and lower springs, is a small picture of a child asking a father for good gifts and receiving abundantly, an echo of how God delights to give good things to those who ask.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. Judah's large and detailed nachalah is received as God's gift by promise. As the royal tribe from whom the Messiah would come, Genesis 49:10, Judah is given its portion first, and its careful, city-by-city record testifies that God kept His promise to settle His people in the land in concrete, nameable fullness.

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, dispossess, drive out. The chapter ends by admitting that Judah could not yarash the Jebusites from Jerusalem. The same verb that runs triumphantly through the conquest here marks a failure, an incomplete obedience that leaves a pagan stronghold in the very city where God would one day set His King, a gap the true Son of Judah would finally close.

basic.context: Judah, the tribe of the coming King, is the first to receive its inheritance, and it is the largest. The chapter carefully traces Judah's borders, then tells a vivid story: Caleb takes Hebron and drives out the giants, and offers his daughter Acsah to whoever captures the town of Debir. His nephew Othniel does it and wins Acsah, who then boldly asks her father not just for dry land but for springs of water, and Caleb generously gives her both upper and lower springs. Then comes a long list of Judah's cities in every region, south, foothills, hill country, and wilderness. But the chapter ends on a sober note: Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, so they remained. The question underneath is: how does God's faithful gift of the land sit alongside His people's incomplete obedience?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, mostly a legal land record with two narrative episodes. The detailed geography testifies concretely to God's faithfulness. The Acsah story models bold, believing petition to a generous father. The closing failure to take Jerusalem is a candid admission of incomplete obedience, part of a recurring pattern in Joshua and Judges that we should not gloss over; it points forward to the need for a greater deliverer.
basic.originalLanguages: Judah receives its nachalah, its inheritance, first and largest. Acsah asks her father for a berakhah, a blessing, and receives springs in abundance. And the chapter ends admitting Judah could not yarash, drive out, the Jebusites from Jerusalem.
basic.typology: Judah as the leading, royal tribe points to Christ, the Lion of Judah, the King who comes from this line. Acsah's bold request to a generous father pictures the confidence with which God's children may ask Him for good gifts. And the unconquered Jerusalem points ahead to the true Son of David who will claim that city and secure the true inheritance.
basic.christ: Judah is the tribe of the Messiah; from it comes David and, at last, Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Revelation 5:5. The very Jerusalem that Judah could not fully take would become the city of David and the place where Christ would die and rise, so that the incompleteness here points to the completeness of what Christ accomplishes. Acsah's springs foreshadow the living water Christ freely gives.
basic.god: God is faithful, giving Judah a full and detailed inheritance just as He promised. He is generous, delighting in the bold request and answering abundantly, as pictured in Caleb's gift of springs. And He is patient and purposeful, leaving even the failure at Jerusalem within His larger plan to bring the true King from Judah.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 49 promises the scepter will not depart from Judah. Judges 1 retells Caleb, Othniel, and Acsah, and the ongoing failure to drive out the Canaanites. 2 Samuel 5 records David finally taking Jerusalem from the Jebusites. And Revelation 5 names Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah.
basic.oneStory: Judah, the royal tribe, receives its inheritance first, a concrete testimony to God's faithfulness, and within it faith is rewarded and generosity shown. Yet the unconquered Jebusites in Jerusalem mark the incompleteness of Israel's obedience. Both the promise and the gap point forward to the Son of Judah, Jesus, who claims the city and secures the inheritance forever.

context.literary:
No other tribal allotment in Joshua receives anything close to this chapter's length or structural elaboration, a literary fact that mirrors Judah's narrative priority everywhere else in the Pentateuch and Former Prophets: Judah is the tribe whose brothers are told they will praise him, Genesis 49:8, the tribe stationed on the leading side of Israel's wilderness camp, Numbers 2:3, and later the first tribe commissioned to fight when Israel needs a champion after Joshua's death, Judges 1:1-2.

The chapter is built in four movements: a formal boundary survey moving from the southern tip of the Salt Sea around to the Mediterranean coast, verses 1 to 12; a narrative interlude about Caleb, Othniel, and Acsah, verses 13 to 19; an unusually organized city catalogue divided into four named geographic zones, the Negev, the foothills, the hill country, and the wilderness, each closing with its own subtotal of cities, verses 20 to 62; and a single closing verse admitting Jerusalem's Jebusites were never dislodged, verse 63.

The Acsah episode deliberately echoes the previous chapter's Caleb episode: just as Caleb asked Joshua for the hill country already promised him and received it, so his own daughter asks him for water already implied by her dowry land and receives even more than she asked, a small family pattern of bold, successful petition repeated across two generations within two consecutive chapters.
context.historical:
Judah's territory as surveyed here stretches across four distinct ecological zones, each demanding a different way of life: the arid Negev in the south, good mainly for herding; the Shephelah foothills, a contested buffer strip that would remain a battleground between Israel and Philistia for centuries, the setting of Samson's exploits and David's duel with Goliath; the hill country proper, Judah's secure heartland, including Hebron and Debir; and the barren wilderness along the Dead Sea's western shore, including En-gedi, verse 62, an oasis where David would later hide from Saul in caves still found today, 1 Samuel 24:1-3.

Debir's older name, Kiriath-sepher, means something like city of the document or city of the scribe, hinting that the town may have functioned as an archive or scribal center under its earlier Canaanite rulers before Othniel captured it. The coastal cities listed in verses 45 to 47, Ekron, Ashdod, and Gaza, belonged to the Philistine confederation that Joshua 13 had already admitted remained unconquered; their inclusion here describes Judah's ideal, promised extent rather than territory Judah actually controlled at the time of writing, the same already-and-not-yet pattern chapter 13 established for the whole land.

Jerusalem, named on Judah's very border in verse 8 and again in the closing verse 63, sat at a strategic highland crossroads that would remain a Jebusite stronghold for roughly another four centuries, until David finally took it.
context.canonical:
Judah's priority here is not a narrative accident; it fulfills Jacob's deathbed word that the scepter would not depart from Judah until the one to whom it belongs comes, Genesis 49:10, a promise this chapter begins to make good on by giving Judah the largest and most fully documented inheritance of any tribe. The Acsah episode is retold almost verbatim in Judges 1:11-15, one of the rare instances where two biblical books preserve nearly identical wording for the same story, a sign of how carefully this small family narrative of bold asking and generous giving was preserved as it passed between the two books.

Jerusalem's mention here, first as a boundary marker in verse 8 and then as the site of failure in verse 63, opens a canonical thread that runs the length of Scripture. The city is glimpsed centuries earlier under its priest-king Melchizedek, Genesis 14:18-20, taken at last by David, 2 Samuel 5:6-9, built up by Solomon as the site of the temple, wept over by Jesus for not knowing the things that make for peace, Luke 19:41-42, and finally transformed in the New Testament's vision into something no earthly army ever took by force, a heavenly Jerusalem that already exists above, Galatians 4:26 and Hebrews 12:22, and a new Jerusalem yet to descend from God completely, Revelation 21:2. The gap this chapter admits in verse 63 is the first recorded chapter of that long story, not its last word.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapter aims to do two things that sit uneasily side by side and are meant to: establish beyond dispute that Judah received a vast, detailed, divinely ordered inheritance, while refusing to hide the one significant failure inside it. By naming roughly one hundred named towns across four regions, the author leaves no room to claim the record is impressionistic; this is meant to be checkable, nameable, real.

Placing the Acsah episode near the front of the chapter, before the long lists begin, also seems calculated to keep the record from feeling merely administrative: readers meet a family, a marriage, a bold request, and a generous answer before they are asked to wade through dozens of unfamiliar place names, so that the human warmth of verses 13 to 19 colors how the rest of the catalogue is read.

And by ending, deliberately, on the single sentence about the Jebusites rather than on a triumphant summary, the author signals that Judah's story, like Israel's as a whole, includes real, unresolved business alongside real, documented blessing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The boundary and city lists are a historical record of one tribe's settlement and prescribe no template for land claims today. The Acsah narrative, likewise, is not a rule about dowries or family customs but an illustration: a daughter's boldness and a father's generosity, held up as a small picture of how petition and blessing are meant to work between a child and a good parent.

What does carry forward as instruction is the honesty modeled in verse 63; Scripture records Judah's failure to remove the Jebusites without excusing it or hiding it behind the chapter's larger success, teaching readers that a substantially faithful record can still include acknowledged, unresolved compromise, and that acknowledging such compromise plainly, rather than glossing over it, is itself part of walking faithfully with God.

debates.question: Why does Acsah ask specifically for springs rather than more land?

views.label: Practical shrewdness given Negev conditions
views.case: The Negev land Caleb had already given her was dry, so springs of water were the single resource that would make the ground she already owned productive; her request is less a demand for more territory than the missing ingredient that turns existing land into a livelihood, a shrewd, specific ask rather than a vague appeal for wealth.

views.label: A statement about the nature of blessing itself
views.case: Acsah's chosen word, give me a blessing, before naming the specific request, frames the springs less as a negotiated asset than as an act of favor from a father who has already shown he gives generously; on this reading the passage is less about water management than about modeling how God's children may ask boldly for a blessing, trusting a generous father to give more than the bare minimum.

debates.bearing: The two readings need not compete: Acsah's practical need and her theological framing of the request as a blessing work together, since it is precisely ordinary, practical need that becomes the occasion for a fuller display of a father's generosity than strict justice would have required.

debates.question: What is the significance of the note that Judah could not drive out the Jebusites?

views.label: An honest record of incomplete obedience
views.case: The same failure will recur and multiply through Judges, and the historian records it here without comment or excuse, letting the bare fact of continued Jebusite presence in Judah's own territory speak for itself as a warning against declaring premature victory.

views.label: The first note in a story that ends with David
views.case: The persistence of this unresolved detail across Joshua, Judges, and into 2 Samuel suggests the author is less interested in blaming this particular generation than in tracking a single loose thread that only the tribe's own future king will finally tie off, turning an admitted failure into the setup for a much larger promise.

debates.bearing: Both readings are true at once: the note is a real, sober admission of failure with real consequences, and it is also, in the shape of the whole biblical story, an open door through which David, and beyond him great David's greater Son, will eventually walk.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's boundary survey runs on one recurring word, gvul, border or territory, used so often across verses 1 to 12 that an ancient hearer would have felt the sheer scale of what is being measured, an unbroken line traced from the Dead Sea's southern tip to the Mediterranean coast. The same word for border elsewhere describes the fixed limits God sets for the sea, Job 38:10-11, so that a boundary in Hebrew thought is never arbitrary line-drawing but the kind of ordered limit God Himself imposes on creation; Judah's border is drawn with the same theological seriousness.

The chapter's four regional names are themselves descriptive rather than merely local. Negev, the southern zone, carries an underlying sense of dryness or parched ground, matching exactly the terrain Acsah receives and finds insufficient without water. Shephelah, rendered foothills, comes from a root meaning to be low, distinguishing this contested lowland strip from the true hill country further inland, a distinction the chapter itself preserves by grouping its city lists under these very regional headings rather than mixing them together.

A smaller but telling detail sits behind the word translated villages throughout the city lists, along with their villages, repeated after nearly every regional total. The underlying idiom is literally daughters, so that Lachish, for instance, is pictured with her daughters clustered around her, smaller dependent settlements drawing life and protection from a larger mother city. The image quietly domesticates what could otherwise read as a dry administrative record, turning a list of conquered territory into a picture of towns and their satellite villages living in family-like relation to one another.

Finally, Acsah's request itself is built on a double use of the verb give, give me, repeated twice in one short speech, first for a blessing generally and then specifically for springs of water. The repetition is an emphatic form of ordinary request in Hebrew speech, not timid but direct, a daughter who knows exactly what she wants and states it plainly to a father already inclined to give. Caleb's response matches the emphasis of the ask: not one spring but both, upper and lower, springs he did not have to give and gave anyway.

typology.type: Judah, the leading tribe, first to receive its promised inheritance
typology.fulfillment: Jacob's blessing over Judah, a young lion who need not fear rousing, and the scepter that will not depart from him until the one to whom it belongs comes, Genesis 49:9-10, moves through this chapter's priority toward its fulfillment when the elders around God's throne announce that the Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed, Revelation 5:5. The correspondence deepens rather than merely repeats: Judah received cities and boundary lines, real but earthly and eventually lost to exile, while the Lion of Judah in Revelation receives the authority to open a scroll containing the destiny of the whole earth.

typology.type: Acsah's bold request answered with more than she asked
typology.fulfillment: Jesus tells His hearers that if flawed earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him, Matthew 7:9-11, and later offers the Samaritan woman living water that becomes in the drinker a spring welling up to eternal life, John 4:13-14, and stands at the feast crying out, if anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink, John 7:37-38. Caleb's gift of both upper and lower springs, beyond what his daughter even named, becomes a small, dry-country picture of a generosity Christ offers on an entirely different scale.

typology.type: The Jebusite stronghold Judah could not take
typology.fulfillment: The very city listed here as unconquered becomes, within a few centuries, the fortress David captures through a hidden water shaft and renames the City of David, 2 Samuel 5:6-9 and 1 Chronicles 11:4-6. Zechariah later pictures Jerusalem's true King entering it humbly, righteous and victorious, riding on a donkey, Zechariah 9:9, a scene the Gospels stage exactly, even as Jesus weeps over the same city for not knowing the things that make for peace, Luke 19:41-42. The type is only completed beyond earthly Jerusalem altogether, in the new Jerusalem descending prepared as a bride, where no enemy will ever again need driving out, Revelation 21:2.

study.christ:
Judah's greatness in this chapter is always borrowed, never intrinsic; the tribe is blessed because from it will come a king, not because Judah's own warriors or wells make it deserving above its brothers. That borrowed greatness culminates in an unlikely place. Micah, centuries later, names not the great cities catalogued in this chapter but a town too small even to be listed here by name, Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among the clans of Judah, as the origin of the one whose goings forth are from everlasting, Micah 5:2. The tribe that receives a hundred named cities in Joshua 15 will one day be defined, in the world's eyes, by an obscure village none of its surveyors thought worth recording.

Jerusalem's mention on Judah's border carries its own layer of foreshadowing that reaches back before Judah even existed as a tribe. The earliest biblical glimpse of the city comes centuries before Joshua, when Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses Abraham, Genesis 14:18-20, a strange, brief appearance the writer of Hebrews later reads as a foretaste of Christ's own priesthood, a priest-king with no recorded genealogy whose order outlasts Levi's, Hebrews 7:1-3. The very city Judah cannot fully claim in verse 63 already carried, long before either Judah or David existed, a priestly-royal pattern that only Christ, priest and king together, would finally embody without remainder.

The chapter's inheritance is also, by definition, bounded, acre by acre and village by village, however generous. The Psalms promise a Son who receives an inheritance without such boundaries at all, ask of Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession, Psalm 2:8. Judah's careful borders, drawn from the Salt Sea to the Great Sea, describe a real but limited gift; the greater Son of Judah receives an inheritance with no coastline, no southern border, and no Jebusite corner left unclaimed, because every nation, not one tribal territory, finally belongs to Him.
study.god:
The God behind this chapter cares about scale in both directions at once. He gives Judah the largest inheritance of any tribe, a boundary line that takes twelve verses simply to trace, and He also cares about each small dependent village clustered around every town, remembered in the text as that town's daughters rather than left uncounted. Nothing is too vast for His attention and nothing too minor to be worth naming; a God who tallies twenty-nine cities in one district and fourteen in the next is not glossing generalities but attending to particulars.

He is also, through Caleb's example, revealed as a generous father before He is ever named as one directly. Caleb does not merely grant his daughter's specific request, springs of water; he gives her both the upper and the lower springs, exceeding what she asked. Scripture elsewhere treats human fatherly generosity as a window onto God's own character, if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more your Father in heaven, so that this small domestic scene, tucked inside a chapter of borders and city lists, quietly teaches what kind of God stands behind the whole inheritance being described.

He is sovereign even over what the chapter admits went wrong. Judah's failure to remove the Jebusites from Jerusalem is not hidden from the record, yet neither does it derail God's larger purpose for that city; the very stronghold Judah could not take in this chapter will, in God's timing, become the capital of Judah's own greatest king. God's plans are not fragile enough to be wrecked by one generation's incomplete obedience, however real that incompleteness is and however seriously the text takes it.

Finally, He is a God unimpressed by the very greatness this chapter records. The tribe given the most detailed inheritance in the whole book will, in the end, be represented before the world not by any of these fortified cities but by an insignificant village too small to earn a place on this list at all.

crossReferences.note: Jacob's blessing over his son promises that Judah's brothers will praise him and that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the one to whom it belongs comes. Judah's priority in receiving the first and largest inheritance in Joshua 15 is the first concrete installment of this deathbed word.

Judah is stationed on the east side of Israel's wilderness camp, the leading position from which the whole company set out on the march. Its priority in Joshua's allotment of the land continues a precedence the tribe already held decades earlier in the wilderness.

After Joshua's death Judah is again named first to lead the ongoing conquest, and the Othniel and Acsah story is retold almost word for word from Joshua 15. The near-identical repetition across two books shows how carefully Israel preserved this small family narrative of bold request and generous reward.

David hides from Saul among the caves of En-gedi, one of the six wilderness towns listed at the close of this chapter's allotment. The barren district assigned to Judah here later becomes the setting where its future king survives his own testing years before the throne.

David finally captures the Jebusite stronghold that Judah's own allotment admits it never took, using a water shaft to surprise the defenders, and renames it the City of David. The gap left open at the end of Joshua 15 closes only once David, the son of Judah, becomes king.

Centuries after this chapter records Judah's many named cities, the prophet singles out a village too small to appear on any such list, Bethlehem Ephrathah, as the birthplace of the ruler whose origins are from everlasting. Judah's true glory ends up resting on a town its own conquest generation never thought to record.

Jesus asks which father would give his son a stone when asked for bread, arguing that if flawed earthly fathers know how to give good gifts, the Father in heaven gives even more generously to those who ask. Caleb's gift of both springs to Acsah, beyond her actual request, is this principle already at work centuries earlier.

At the feast Jesus cries out that anyone who is thirsty may come to Him and drink, promising that streams of living water will flow from within the believer. Acsah's request for springs to water her dry Negev land quietly anticipates a thirst only Christ can finally satisfy.

One of the elders announces that the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed and is worthy to open the scroll. The tribe given priority in dividing an earthly land in Joshua 15 is given, in the end, authority over the destiny of the whole earth.

John sees the new Jerusalem descending from God, prepared as a bride, replacing forever the city Judah could never fully secure by conquest. What verse 63 leaves as an open wound in Israel's history, Revelation heals completely, with no Jebusite corner and no unfinished business left standing.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ends with a dying Jacob gathering his sons to bless them, and Judah receives more than blessing; he receives a scepter and a coming ruler, a promise that at the time cost the tribe nothing and asked for nothing in return, Genesis 49:8-10. By the time Joshua 15 is written, that unearned promise has become an enormous, itemized inheritance, the largest of any tribe, proof across centuries and two books that a promise spoken once in a deathbed blessing had not weakened with age.

Yet the very inheritance that proves God's faithfulness also exposes, in a single closing verse, the limits of Judah's own obedience. The chapter cannot end simply as celebration; it must end with a Jebusite fortress still standing inside territory God had already given, a small but honest crack in an otherwise triumphant record. That crack does not close on its own. It takes centuries and another son of Judah, David, before the city is finally secured, and even then only as a foretaste of something greater still to come.

Between those two poles, promise given and promise not yet fully realized, the chapter drops one bright, human scene: a daughter asking her father for water in a dry land and receiving more than she requested. It is a small mercy inside a much larger story of land and lineage, but it is not incidental; every good gift Scripture records between a father and a child, all the way back to the garden and all the way forward to the gospel, points toward the same generous character.

The story that begins with Judah's scepter promised in Genesis, runs through this chapter's borders and city lists, and passes through David's capture of the last unconquered corner, arrives finally at a Lion of Judah who needs no further conquest, and at a city descending rather than being stormed, because every enemy still standing in Joshua 15 has, by then, been put down for good.

quiz.q: Why does Judah receive its inheritance first and in the greatest detail?

options.text: Because Judah is the leading, royal tribe from which the Messiah would come.
options.note: Judah's priority reflects Jacob's blessing that the scepter would come from Judah, Genesis 49:10.

options.text: Because Judah had the most warriors of any tribe.
options.note: Judah was prominent, but its priority rests on its royal, Messianic calling, not merely army size.

options.text: Because Judah paid the most for its land.
options.note: No payment was involved; the inheritance was God's gift, and Judah's place is its royal role.

options.text: Because the other tribes refused their portions.
options.note: The other tribes received their portions too; Judah's priority is due to its royal calling.

quiz.q: What did Acsah ask her father Caleb for, and what did she receive?

options.text: She boldly asked for springs of water in addition to her land, and Caleb gave her both upper and lower springs.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 show her bold request and Caleb's generous answer.

options.text: She asked only for the dry Negev land and got nothing more.
options.note: She already had the land; she asked for and received the springs as well.

options.text: She demanded her father's whole estate.
options.note: She asked for a blessing of springs, not the entire estate.

options.text: She refused any gift from her father.
options.note: The opposite: she asked boldly and received generously.

quiz.q: How does the chapter honestly end regarding Jerusalem?

options.text: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, who remained in Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 63 candidly records the incomplete conquest of Jerusalem.

options.text: Judah fully conquered Jerusalem and settled it.
options.note: The opposite: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites; Jerusalem was not yet fully taken.

options.text: Judah destroyed Jerusalem completely and left it in ruins.
options.note: Jerusalem was not destroyed; the Jebusites remained living there among Judah.

options.text: Jerusalem was given to another tribe entirely.
options.note: Jerusalem lay on Judah's border; the note is that Judah could not drive out its Jebusite inhabitants.

quiz.q: How does the unconquered Jerusalem point forward in Scripture?

options.text: David, the son of Judah, would later take it, and it would become the city of the great King and the place of Christ's death and resurrection.
options.note: The gap is filled by David in 2 Samuel 5 and ultimately by Christ, the Son of Judah.

options.text: It shows that God's plan for Jerusalem had permanently failed.
options.note: The opposite: the unfinished conquest sets up David and Christ; God's plan advanced, it did not fail.

options.text: It means Jerusalem would never matter in the Bible again.
options.note: Jerusalem becomes central to the rest of Scripture as the city of the King.

options.text: It teaches that incomplete obedience never has consequences.
options.note: The incomplete conquest did have consequences; it exposed a real failure that pointed to the need for a greater deliverer.

questions: The chapter records Judah's inheritance down to the smallest village, testifying to God's faithfulness in detail. Where do you need to remember that God keeps His promises concretely, not just in general?
Acsah boldly asked her father for more than the bare minimum and received abundantly. How does her example encourage you to ask your heavenly Father boldly for good gifts?
Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, leaving unfinished business that would cause trouble later. Where in your life is incomplete obedience leaving a stronghold that needs to be dealt with?
The very city Judah could not take became the city of the King and the place of the cross. How does it comfort you that God works even through your failures toward His good purposes?
Judah is the tribe of the Lion, Jesus. How does knowing that all these details lead to Christ deepen your reading even of a chapter full of place names?

translationNotes.note: The Jebusites, that is, Jerusalem, are named on Judah's boundary here and again in verse 63; the city would not be fully taken until David, 2 Samuel 5.
The BSB footnote notes a textual variant, that some manuscripts read he urged her rather than she urged him; the parallel is Judges 1:14.
Acsah's request for springs reflects the dryness of the Negev land she received; the upper and lower springs would make it fruitful.
